operation_details.item: The user uses Google Fonts as one of their type sources.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Hi there! I saw you're working on a brand identity refresh for the bakery client. How's the type direction coming along?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: It's going well! I'm exploring display faces for the logo and packaging. For the body text I'll pull from my usual library—I use Adobe Fonts for most client work.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Adobe Fonts is a solid choice for reliability. Are you considering anything more distinctive for the display type?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Yes, for the display I want something hand-drawn with character. I buy direct foundry licenses for display faces so we can really stand out.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That makes sense—direct licenses give you more flexibility for custom lettering. How do you keep track of all the different licenses across projects?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I keep a spreadsheet that my studio shares with the PMs. All client typefaces are logged in the license tracker.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Great system. And when you need a quick web font for a prototype or a smaller client, what's your go-to?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: For lightweight projects I often use open source options. I use Google Fonts as one of my type sources.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Nice—having that mix of commercial and open-source sources really helps with budget alignment. Are you also matching the Google Font with any of the Adobe Fonts for the web mockup?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Exactly. I'll pair it with a clean sans from Adobe Fonts for the UI, while the display is the direct license.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That sounds like a balanced system. Do you find that foundry-specific licensing terms ever conflict with your client's usage limits?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Occasionally, so I always double-check the license before sending final files. It's easier when everything is documented in the tracker.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Smart. What about the hand-drawn lettering? Are you illustrating it yourself or commissioning a type designer?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I'm commissioning a foundry that does custom lettering—actually it's a small independent type foundry, so the direct license will cover the custom work.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That will give the brand a unique voice. When do you need to deliver the first round of options?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: The client wants initial concepts by Monday, so I'm narrowing down the display choices this afternoon. After that I'll log the final selection in the license tracker.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Sounds like a solid plan. Let me know if you need any help organizing the presentation for the client.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Thanks, I will! I'll send you the presentation outline later today.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That is helpful context.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I buy direct foundry licenses for display faces.
